chapter_theme: The kurinji courtship's second half: the man's pleas, in which the girl's eyes are spears and arrows and her family hunters and clearers of the hill (17, 19, 21-23, 30); the friend's refusals and warnings, of leaf-garment and night visit, with the vengai that is both gold-flowered tree and tiger (20, 24-26, 28); and the end of the field-watch, the harvest, the mother's guard and the push to marry (18, 27, 29, 31).

17.reading: The man tells the friend that he knows the girl with the slender waist, fears it will snap if she walks even a little, and, finding no moment when she grants him even a little kindness, his heart melts and sways wherever she sways.
17.nuance: The verse turns on ஒல்கு: she sways as she walks, and his heart sways with her, so his surrender copies her gait. Her fragility is praise, and the fear that her waist will break is his own helplessness projected onto her.

thinai_evidence.note: a man pleading for a girl's favour before any union is the kurinji situation of courtship

18.reading: The speaker asks what will become of it: the peerless young vengai, turning gold, has announced the day, the spear-bearing kin have settled on what they will do, and now the millet field will be stubble, and with it the bond with the hill lord.
18.nuance: The vengai's flowering was the sign for the harvest, and once the millet is cut the girl no longer goes out to guard it; so the young tree 'announcing the day' is the clock that ends the secret meetings. மருவியா மாலை may be 'the evening not shared' or 'the garland not worn'.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai's bloom and the millet field fix the field-watch of kurinji

19.reading: The man says that the eyes of the girl who, after leaping and bathing in a white fall like milk, guards the mountain rice that looks strewn with many flowers, entered his heart like a spear; will they ever let it go? He aches for the gentle one who will not let herself be seen.
19.nuance: Three likenesses with the same marker build the scene from the outside in: the fall, the field, and then the eye, which ends inside him. The girl is busy guarding a field, yet it is he who is overrun.

thinai_evidence.note: the waterfall and the mountain rice the girl watches are kurinji things

20.reading: The friend tells the lord of the good hill, where the vengai yields gold on its day, that her brothers are cruel like killing tigers and the mother too is a tiger, so they cannot take his rare leaf-garment; what excuse will come easy tomorrow?
20.nuance: The verse plays on வேங்கை, the gold-flowering kino tree of line 1 and the killing tiger of lines 2 and 3: the same word that gives the hill its beauty gives the family its menace. Refusing the leaf-garment is refusing the suit for now; 'tomorrow' hints that refusal cannot go on.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai, the hill and the leaf-garment offered are the kurinji courtship

21.reading: The girl whose body puts gold to shame has soft breasts with flower-like spots that swelled as he wasted, the man complains, calling it a wrong; since she does not fade at his fading he cannot bear it, while the kohl-eyed girl, though vexed, does not fade.
21.nuance: The symmetry is the point: her body grows as his shrinks, so her ripening looks to him like a theft from his own body. Who speaks lines 3 and 4 is unclear; read as the friend reporting his complaint, the last line turns it gently against the girl.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover wasting while the girl ripens belongs to courtship before union

22.reading: The man tells the girl that her rich brothers gather the white tusks of killing elephants and the skins of strong killing tigers, bringing each beast down with a single arrow, but she today has shot him with two arrows so that he cannot leave.
22.nuance: One arrow against two: the brothers' skill is real, but she needs twice their shots to bring him down and still he does not go. ஈரம்பு can also be heard as 'a moist arrow', the wet bright eye.

thinai_evidence.note: the elephant and tiger hunted by her hill kin place it in kurinji

23.reading: The man says that for the lovely breasts of the sister of men who search the great hills, take their fill of honey and then carelessly ruin what was hard to reach, he is one fit to lose his shame, his good looks and his standing, melting away.
23.nuance: The brothers take the honey and destroy what held it; the poem sets that beside the man's own ruin by their sister, so he feels himself used and spent the same way. அருமலை is hard: 'the hard-to-reach hill' or the hive on it.

thinai_evidence.note: honey-gathering on the great hills is the hill people's work

comparisons.tenor: the girl's undoing of the man

24.reading: The friend tells the man to consider whether the sister of men who, wanting only what they want, cut down fragrant cool thakaram and vakulam as if they were worthless bush and plough the ground to sow red millet could ever grieve and pine for another's pain.
24.nuance: The friend turns the family's farming into a character sketch: people who fell fragrance for grain do not keep pity for an outsider's pain. Read as the man's own complaint, the verse would be a lover's bitterness rather than a refusal; the speaker is inferred.

thinai_evidence.note: clearing the slope for red millet is the hill farmers' work of kurinji

25.reading: The friend tells the man that the gentle girl with eyes like dread spears trembles, like an elephant of killing nature that has escaped the grip of the curve-striped tiger and goes looking for its own good herd; let him not come by night bearing his guarding spear.
25.nuance: The simile gives the girl the elephant's state after danger, still shaking as it looks for safety: her fear outlasts each of his visits. His spear, ஏமவேல், is meant to protect, but it cannot protect her from fearing for him.

thinai_evidence.note: the elephant and the tiger of the slope are kurinji beasts

comparisons.tenor: the girl trembling for the night visitor

26.reading: The friend tells the man that on the cloud-fed slope the flowers the dark-trunked young vengai has dropped look like a big-pawed strong tiger, and if he comes by night she whose soft grace is set off by her jewels will not live.
26.nuance: Again the two வேங்கை: the tree's spotted heap of flowers looks like the tiger of the same name, so even a false tiger is enough to kill the girl with fear for him. The danger is in her mind, not on the path, and that is the friend's argument.

thinai_evidence.note: the slope and the night visit are kurinji's place and hour

27.reading: The friend tells the lord of the good fruitful hill with tall vengai on its misty peaks that she speaks to urge him to marry now: when he came, relying on one who stood in the hill, mother saw him, and, displeased, she has angrily set a watch on the girl.
27.nuance: The friend's 'now' (இனி) has a cause: the secret is out to the mother and the girl is kept in, so the only way left to meet her is marriage. முனிவரையுள் நின்றான் is obscure: a god of the hill whom he trusted, or a man who stood guard.

thinai_evidence.note: the misty peak and fruitful hill are the kurinji land

28.reading: Having seen the great wide eyes of the sister of men who cut down cloud-touching sandal, thimisu, hard-cored agil and the sky-high naagam and plough the ground, would any man who knew wander about this hill, the friend asks.
28.nuance: The list of precious trees felled without regret is a portrait of the brothers: what they do to sandal and agil they would do to a stranger. The question can also be heard as wonder at the man's daring, since he does wander the hill though he knows.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill trees felled for millet ploughing belong to kurinji

29.reading: The speaker points out the place: by the bed of milky varukkai jackfruit trees a long stretch of sand white as risen moonlight, and where the forest stream, swirling up, has cut a channel, a cool thicket of glory lilies hangs low and fills it with scent.
29.nuance: The verse is only a place, with no person named: read as the friend telling the man where to meet, every detail is a sign of shelter (low branches, scent, soft sand). The site's text lacks the first line, so this reading rests on our text alone.

thinai_evidence.note: jackfruit, forest stream and glory lily are kurinji things

30.reading: The man says that her kin, drawing a bow upon the moon and holding back the spear without thought, and holding her cheaply as one of their own, set the flower-haired girl here to guard the millet field, and so, without knowing it, set her to guard his heart.
30.nuance: The wit is in the double posting: the family sends her out to keep birds from the millet, and in doing so posts her over his heart, which she now holds. Line 1 is dense; the bow on the moon is most easily her brows on her face and the spear held back her eyes.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl set to guard the millet field is the kurinji field-watch

comparisons.tenor: her brows on her moon-like face

31.reading: The friend tells the girl that the lord of the cool slope brings leaves, never saying it is his own need but thinking only of hers; yet he does not come into the shade of the vengai whose gold is now thinning; what can he mean, this man like a killing tiger?
31.nuance: The friend praises his tact (he brings the gift as if it were her need, not his) and in the same breath worries: the vengai's blossoms are falling, the season of meeting is passing, and he keeps away. Calling him a tiger is praise of his strength and a hint that he is hard to read.

thinai_evidence.note: the leaf-garment and the vengai of the slope are kurinji courtship

links.note: Both men fear the girl's waist will break: the Kural through the flowers' stems, Thinaimalai 17 if she walks even a little.
links.teaches: The Kural keeps the snapping waist a joke of praise, a mock funeral drum, while Thinaimalai 17 lets the same fear spill into the man's own body, whose heart sways wherever she sways, so the conceit of her fragility becomes a measure of his surrender.

links.note: Thinaimalai 18 fears that the harvested millet ends the bond; in Akananuru 132 the millet ears are already cut and the friend tells the man to take the girl away.
links.teaches: Thinaimalai 18 stops at the fear that the stubble field ends the meetings, and Akananuru 132 shows what the friend does with that fear, turning it into a demand to take the girl away, so the harvest is the point at which kalavu must become marriage or flight.

links.note: The Kural's man asks whether her look is Death; the man of Thinaimalai 22 says her two eyes shot him as her brothers shoot beasts.
links.teaches: The Kural names the killing look in the abstract, and Thinaimalai 22 grounds it in her people's trade, measuring her two eyes against her brothers' single killing arrow, so the deadly glance of the couplet turns out to be a hunter's weapon of the hills.

links.note: Natrinai 13 likens the girl's red-lined eyes to the arrows millet-watchers pull out of a felled beast; Thinaimalai 22 has her eyes as two arrows that have felled the man.
links.teaches: The friend of Natrinai 13 gives the eyes the hunters' bloodied arrows, and the man of Thinaimalai 22 draws the consequence that he is the beast they brought down, so the two poems together show the eye-as-arrow belonging to a hunting household's daily kill.

links.note: Both use the formula of the kin who cut and plough (எறிந்து உழுது, எறிந்தெமர் தாம்உழுத); in Ainthinai Aimpathu 18 it is the field they cleared, in Thinaimalai 24 a sign of their hardness.
links.teaches: In Ainthinai Aimpathu 18 clearing and ploughing is just the kin's labour whose harvest ends the meetings, but Thinaimalai 24 reads the same labour as a temperament, men who fell fragrance for grain, so the friend can turn the hill family's farming into a reason the girl will not pity the man.

links.note: Both show an elephant that has escaped the curve-striped tiger; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 16 it lies hurt on the hero's night path, in Thinaimalai 25 it is the likeness of the trembling girl.
links.teaches: Ainthinai Aimpathu 16 puts the escaped elephant on the man's path as a danger the sleepless girl imagines, and Thinaimalai 25 makes the escaped elephant the girl herself, still shaking after the danger, so one stock scene can stand either for the night road or for the fear it leaves in her.

links.note: In both the fallen vengai flowers look like a tiger: in Akananuru 228 a she-elephant bolts from them on the man's moonlit way home, in Thinaimalai 26 the girl will not survive his night visit.
links.teaches: Akananuru 228 shows the vengai's false tiger frightening a beast on the path, and Thinaimalai 26 transfers that fright to the waiting girl, which shows that the friend's case against the night visit rests on fear of a likeness rather than on any real tiger.

links.note: In Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 10 the girl tells her friend that mother, learning of the union, has barred her from the field; in Thinaimalai 27 the friend tells the man that mother saw him and keeps the girl guarded.
links.teaches: The same discovery by the mother is grief in the girl's mouth, who wonders whether he will be vexed, and a lever in the friend's, who uses it to tell him to marry now, so the confinement that ends kalavu is also the friend's strongest argument for marriage.

links.note: Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 5 warns the man off because the kin carry bows, spears and swift arrows; Thinaimalai 28 warns him through the precious trees the kin cut down to plough.
links.teaches: Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 5 states the threat as weapons, and Thinaimalai 28 leaves weapons out and lets the felled sandal and agil show what the brothers would do to an intruder, so the threat can be carried by how a family treats its own hill rather than by its arms.

links.note: Akananuru 92 forbids the night and promises the man a day meeting by a cool fall where red glory lilies open; Thinaimalai 29 describes such a place by a forest stream in a glory-lily thicket.
links.teaches: Akananuru 92 gives the day tryst as the friend's offer in exchange for the dangerous night, and Thinaimalai 29 gives only the place, which shows the daytime meeting ground was a fixed set (stream, glory lilies, low shade) a four-line verse could call up without the bargain around it.

links.note: Both turn on the leaf-garment and the pun on வேங்கை (kino tree and tiger); in 20 the tigers are the girl's brothers and mother and the gift is refused, in 31 the tiger is the man himself and his gift is praised.
links.teaches: Read together, the friend moves the tiger from the girl's family to her lover as she moves from turning the leaf-garment away to pressing the girl toward him, so the same pun marks which side of the courtship holds the danger at each stage.

source_issues: 17-31: the core records carry no colophon thurai, so thurai_akam speaker, addressee and stage are inferred from the poems and occasion.words is null throughout.
17 line 1: அறி(கு)அவளை ஐய இடைம்மடவாய் ஆயச் is hard to construe; read as 'I know her, the slender-waisted one, O girl', with the doubled ம் in இடைம்மடவாய் probably a misprint.
19 line 1: பாலெத்த is probably பாலொத்த ('like milk'), matching தாலொத்த and வேலொத்து in the next line.
21: the speaker and construction of lines 3 and 4 (அண்கண்ணி, ஆற்றான்) are unclear; the reading is tentative.
23 line 2: அருமலை is obscure ('the hard-to-reach hill' or the hives on it).
26 line 1: கள்மேல் may be கல்மேல் ('on the rock'), where the fallen vengai flowers would lie; as printed it is 'on the honey'.
29 line 1: flagged site_diff; the site's text lacks line 1, which stands in our text.
